terms.gloss: dung-pit, muck heap: the compost heap
evidence: Cato Agr. 5.8: stercilīnum magnum studē ut habeās
Varr. RR 1.13.4: Secundum vīllam duo habēre oportet stercilīna (Lewis & Short)
Col. 1.6.21: Sterquilīnia quoque duo sint (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: The farm’s heap of dung, straw, and leaves, kept to rot down and be spread on the fields: what the house keeps today as a compost heap. Cato and Varro write it stercilīnum, Phaedrus sterquilīnum; Lewis & Short’s headword is sterquilīnium. Varro and Columella want two, one filling and one rotted and ready to cart out. In Plautus and Terence it is also a term of abuse (Lewis & Short).

phrases.english: Throw the peelings on the compost heap.

phrases.latin: Stercilīnum magnum studē ut habeās. Stercus sēdulō cōnservā.
phrases.english: Be sure to have a big compost heap. Save the muck carefully.

phrases.latin: Sterquilīnia quoque duo sint: ūnum, quod nova pūrgāmenta recipiat et in annum cōnservet; alterum, ex quō vetera vehantur.
phrases.english: There should also be two dung heaps: one to take the fresh sweepings and keep them for a year, the other from which the old is carted away.

phrases.latin: in sterquilīnō pullus gallīnāceus dum quaerit ēscam, margarītam repperit
phrases.english: a young cockerel, looking for food on the dung heap, found a pearl

sources: Lewis & Short: sterquilinium · Lewis & Short: fimetum
